title: Directory
body:
There are two kinds of paths
Relative and absolute.

An **absolute** path starts at the root and works everywhere: `/users/ewse/1633/a1`. A
**relative** path starts wherever you currently are: `1633/a1`, `../`, `./a.out`. `pwd`
tells you where "here" is, which is the thing that makes relative paths behave.

| | Means |
|---|---|
| `.` | this directory |
| `..` | the one above |
| `~` | your home directory |
| `/` | the root, and the separator |

Moving around and looking: `cd`, `ls -al`, `mkdir`, `rm -r`. All of it in [[Shell]].

The `:.` the course has you add to `PATH` in your [[Bash file]] is exactly this: it puts `.`
on the search list so a freshly compiled `a.out` is runnable without the `./`.
